Does the same personality carry the same consequences? Personality, race, sex, and school suspension

education
logistic regression
preregistration
NLSY
Add Health
R
In two national longitudinal datasets, Black male students with high trait anger faced sharply elevated suspension risk that White female students did not, while self-reported misbehavior showed no racial gap.
Published

June 1, 2023

In brief. Out-of-school suspension is handed out unevenly by race, and the usual explanation is behavior. I tested a different one: that the same personality trait is read differently depending on who has it. Using 6,351 students from two national longitudinal datasets, with a preregistered analysis plan, I modeled suspension, high school graduation, and college expectations as a function of personality, race, and sex. Trait anger predicted suspension far more strongly for Black boys (OR = 1.93) than for White girls, while self-reported delinquency showed no racial gap. The disparity tracks adult judgment more closely than student behavior.

N = 6,351NLSY79-CYAAdd Healthpreregistered (OSF)three-way interactionssimple slopes

Why this mattered

School discipline disparities are among the most litigated and most studied gaps in American education, and the debate usually stalls on one question: is the gap driven by what students do or by how adults respond? Personality gives a way in. If a trait like anger or low conscientiousness predicts suspension equally for everyone, the behavioral account holds; if the same trait predicts suspension only for some groups, the judgment account gains ground.

Data

NoteAccess

Both datasets are public but registration-gated. Study 1 used the Children and Young Adults of the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1979 (N = 1,255); Study 2 used Add Health Waves I and III (N = 5,096), for a combined analytic sample of 6,351 drawn from roughly 17,000 available records. Personality was measured with the 20-item Mini-IPIP and, in Add Health, NEO-PI-R anger and HPI anxiety and optimism items. Analysis code is public; person-level data are not redistributed.

What I did

The analysis was preregistered at osf.io/79wna. Continuous outcomes (PIAT math percentile) were modeled with OLS and binary outcomes (suspension, graduation, college desire and expectation) with logistic regression, each including the race × sex × trait three-way interaction and simple-slope contrasts for every trait so that the effect of a trait could be read separately within each group.

What I found

Black male students at high trait anger faced sharply elevated suspension risk (OR = 1.93); White female students at the same trait level did not. Self-reported delinquency, the behavioral control, showed no racial gap. The pattern is consistent with suspension disparities reflecting how adults interpret the same disposition in different students.

What a team would do with this

For a district or an education-technology company, the operational implication is that discipline and referral data cannot be treated as a clean measure of behavior; they measure behavior filtered through adult judgment. Any model that uses referrals as an outcome or a feature inherits that filter, and the fix is to model the interaction explicitly rather than adjust for race as a main effect and move on.

Limits

Personality is self-reported and measured once. The two datasets differ in instruments and cohort, so the replication is conceptual, not exact. Interaction effects in logistic models are sensitive to cell sizes, which is why the preregistration fixed the contrasts in advance.
